segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: So, welcome to your introductorygeography lecture.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: We'll begin with some basics.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Firstly, what do we learn by studying geography?

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Well, we learn a great deal about all the processesthat have affected and that continueto affect the earth's surface.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: But we learn far more than that, becausestudying geography 031 also informs us about the different kinds of relationshipsthat develop between a particular environmentand the people that live there. 032 Okay.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: We like to think of geography as having two main branches.There's the study of the nature of our planet - its physicalfeatures, what it actually looks like - and then there's the study of the ways in which we choose to live and of the impact of those on our planet.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Our 033 current use of carbon fuels is a good of that.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: But there are more specific study areas to consider too, and we'll be looking at each of these in turn throughout this semester.These include bio-physicalgeography,by which I mean the study of the natural environmentand all its living things.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Then there's topography - that looks at the shapes of the land and oceans.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: There's the study of political geography and social geographytoo, of course, which is the study of communitiesof people.We have economic geography- in which we examine all kinds of resourcesand their use - agriculture,for .

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Next comes historical geography- the understandingof how people and their environmentsand ·theways they interact have changed over a period of time - and urban geography,an aspect I'm particularlyinterestedin, which takes as its . 034 focus the location of cities, the services that those cities provide,and migrationof people to and from such cities.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: And lastly, we have cartography.That's the art and science of map- making.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: You'll be doing a lot of that!

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: So, to summarise before we continue, we now·have our key answer ... studying this subject is important becausewithout geographicalknowledge,we would know very little about our surroundingsand we wouldn't be able to identify all the problemsthat relateto 035 them.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: So, by definition, we wouldn't be in an informed positionto work out how to solve any of them.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Okay, now for some practicalities.What do geographersactually do?

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Well, we collect data to begin with!

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: You'll be doing a lot of that on your first field trip!

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: How do we do this?

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: There are several means.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: We might, for , conduct a census count a populationin a given area perhaps.We also need images of the earth's surfacewhich we can produce by 036 means of computer-generationtechnology or with the help of satellite relays.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: We've come a very long way from the early explorationof the world by sailing ships when geographers only had pens and paper at their disposal.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: After we've gathered our information,we must analyse it!

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: We need to look for patterns, 037 most commonlythose of causes and consequences.This kind of informationhelps us to predict and resolve problemsthat could affect the world we live in.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: But we don't keep all this informationconfidential.We then need to publish our findings so that other people can access it and be informed by it.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: And one way in which this information can be publishedis in the form of maps.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: You'll all have used one at some stage of your life already.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Let's considerthe benefits of maps from a geographer'sperspective.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Maps can be folded and put in a pocket and can provide a great store of referencewhen they're collected into an atlas.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: They can depict the physical features of the entire planet if necessary,or, just a small part of it in much greater detail.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: But there is a drawback.You can't exactly replicate somethingthat is three-dimensional,like our planet, on a flat piece of paper, because paper has only two dimensions,and that means there'll always be a certain degree of distortion on a map.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: It can't be avoided. 038 We can also use aerial photographs ... picturestaken by camerasat high altitude above the earth.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: These are great for showing all kinds of geographicalfeatures that are not easy to see 'fromthe ground.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: You can easily illustrateareas of diseasedtrees or how much · traffic is on the roads at a given time or informationabout deep sea beds, for . 039 Then there are Landsats.These are satellitesthat circle the earth and transmit visual informationto computers at receivingstations.They circle the earth several times a day and can provide a mass of information you'll all be familiar with the informationthey give us about the weather, for exampl~. 040 So, what we're going to do now is look at a short presentationin which you'll see all these tools ... lilill
